content: Tuberculosis (TB) is an infectious disease caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis. It primarily affects the lungs due to the bacterium's preference for oxygen-rich environments, but it can also involve other systems such as the central nervous system, lymphatic system, circulatory system, genitourinary system, bones, joints, and skin. Over one-third of the global population has been exposed to M. tuberculosis, with new infections occurring at a rate of one per second. However, not all exposed individuals develop active disease; many have asymptomatic, latent TB, which is often detected through screening. Approximately 10% of latent infections progress to active TB, which, if untreated, can have a mortality rate of up to 50%. Symptoms of active TB include shortness of breath, hemoptysis (coughing up blood), fever, chills, night sweats, and weight loss. Treatment for TB varies depending on whether the infection is latent or active. Latent TB is typically treated with a single agent, such as rifampin or isoniazid, for 6–9 months. Active TB requires a more aggressive regimen involving four major anti-tuberculous drugs: rifampin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide. Historically, TB has been present in humans for thousands of years. The earliest confirmed detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis was in bison remains dating back to 18,000 BC. The disease likely originated in cattle and was transmitted to humans or diverged from a common ancestor. TB has been known by various names, including phthisis and wasting disease. Evidence of TB has been found in skeletal deformities of ancient Egyptian mummies from 2400 BC, and written records of the disease date back to 3300–2300 years ago in India and China. During the Middle Ages and Renaissance, TB was referred to as the King’s Evil. The contagious nature and pathology of TB were described during this period. In 1882, Robert Koch identified Mycobacterium tuberculosis, marking a significant milestone in understanding the disease. Effective treatment became possible with the discovery of the antibiotic streptomycin in 1946. However, drug-resistant strains began to emerge in the 1980s. TB is classified into six main categories based on exposure, clinical symptoms, and diagnostic testing. The classification ranges from Class 0 (no exposure or infection) to Class 3 (active TB) and Class 5 (suspected TB). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) uses a classification system based on the disease's pathogenesis to monitor TB progression in patients. Health care providers are required to report cases of Class 3 or Class 5 TB to local or state health departments. Pathophysiologically, TB is a granulomatous infection transmitted through respiratory droplets. Granulomas form to contain the bacteria, preventing their spread and facilitating immune cell communication. Within the granuloma, CD4 T lymphocytes release cytokines like interferon-gamma, which activate macrophages. In immunocompetent individuals, TB is asymptomatic in 90% of cases. Symptomatic patients may present with pulmonary or extrapulmonary manifestations. Primary infections can disseminate, and TB can accelerate the progression of HIV if both infections are present. Clinical manifestations, progression, and prognosis vary depending on the patient’s age and immune status. The causative agent, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is an aerobic, acid-fast bacillus that replicates slowly. It belongs to the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, which includes other species like M. bovis and M. africanum. The bacterium exhibits tropism for lung cells but can infect other species, with humans being its primary natural reservoir. Mortality rates from TB have been steadily decreasing since 1990, but the disease remains more prevalent in older men, racial and ethnic minorities, and individuals co-infected with HIV. In 2015, 60% of global TB cases occurred in six countries: South Africa, Indonesia, Nigeria, Pakistan, India, and China. Risk factors for TB include a weakened immune system (e.g., due to HIV, diabetes, or immunosuppressive medications), close contact with infected individuals, poor hygiene, and a history of previous TB infection. Risk factors for multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) include non-adherence to treatment regimens, insufficient medication, and contact with MDR-TB patients. Screening for TB is commonly performed using the Mantoux tuberculin skin test (TST) or interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs). The Mantoux test involves intradermal injection of a purified protein derivative and monitoring for a reaction. Chest X-rays are a key diagnostic tool, revealing parenchymal and pleural abnormalities such as infiltrates, cavities, fibrosis, and calcifications. Advanced imaging techniques like CT and MRI are used for more detailed assessments, particularly in extrapulmonary TB cases. Echocardiography may be helpful in diagnosing TB-related pericardial effusion or rare cases of congestive heart failure. Treatment of TB involves medical therapy tailored to the patient’s condition. Presumptive treatment may begin even before culture results are available if there is a high probability of infection. Patients typically show improvement within weeks of starting treatment but must be monitored for adverse effects and treatment failure. Drug-resistant TB requires an empirical regimen of at least four drugs based on expert advice. Pediatric TB is particularly concerning due to the risk of life-threatening forms like miliary TB or TB meningitis. Treatment in children is similar to adults but adjusted for weight. Surgical intervention may be necessary in certain cases, such as draining abscesses, stabilizing the spine in Pott’s disease, or resecting affected tissues in abdominal TB. Primary prevention focuses on avoiding disease transmission through measures like respiratory isolation, use of masks, and vaccination with the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine in high-risk populations. Secondary prevention includes early diagnosis and treatment to prevent disease progression. Cost-effective management of TB is crucial, particularly in regions with high disease prevalence. Ambulatory care is preferred over inpatient care unless severe complications arise. Future therapies are being developed to address emerging drug-resistant TB strains, with some new drugs showing promising results in clinical trials.
